intervals and tests executable in base R. Here we return to Chapter 4's group comparisons and use R to connect a fitted model with the question it answers. We begin with three means, compare selected differences, and then examine a six-cell pattern. A separate example adds a pretest so that a group comparison can hold baseline performance fixed. Counts require a different response model. They also provide a small example of likelihood, which makes a fitting criterion explicit. Finally, simulation examines procedures under a stated generating process, and planning relates sample size to either power or interval width. Throughout, a useful result keeps its data, target, uncertainty calculation and conditions together. ::: Chapter 5 made estimates, intervals and tests executable for one mean and for one correlation. Studies rarely stop at one mean. Twelve pupils of the invented feedback study practised in the massed schedule, four in each of three feedback conditions, and their three group means on the 20-item assessment are 6, 8 and 10 correct answers. Means that differ in a record differ for more than one reason, so the question is what a stated model and its conditions let us say about three means at once, and what a single answer to that question leaves unsettled. These pupils are authored teaching inputs allocated by stipulation, so each analysis shows what a procedure reports, not what feedback does. ## Fit and read group means {#ch06-group-models} ### Begin with the question and records Does mean assessment performance differ across three feedback conditions? Chapter 4 developed this question with an invented study of 24 pupils. Each pupil was individually assigned to one combination of feedback (Rereading, Answer feedback or Explanatory feedback) and practice (Massed or Spaced). The outcome is the number correct on a 20-item assessment. Four pupils contribute scores to each cell in @tbl-ch06-feedback-data. | Feedback | Massed scores | Spaced scores | |:--|:--|:--| | Rereading | 4, 5, 7, 8 | 4, 5, 7, 8 | | Answer feedback | 6, 7, 9, 10 | 10, 11, 13, 14 | | Explanatory feedback | 8, 9, 11, 12 | 16, 17, 19, 20 | : The same 24 authored scores as Chapter 4. {#tbl-ch06-feedback-data tbl-colwidths="[35,32,33]"} These values were constructed to make the calculations transparent. They are teaching inputs, not empirical evidence that one feedback condition works better. Each score comes from a different pupil; the four scores within a cell are not repeated measurements of one pupil. Repeated patterns in their deviations were deliberately chosen and cannot establish assumptions about a population. The following code creates the complete data. The factor levels specify the display order and the reference group for subsequent model coefficients. `subset()` selects the twelve pupils assigned to Massed practice; the selected rows still represent twelve distinct pupils. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} feedback_data <- data.frame( student = 1:24, feedback = factor(rep(c("Rereading", "Answer feedback", "Explanatory feedback"), each = 8), levels = c("Rereading", "Answer feedback", "Explanatory feedback")), practice = factor(rep(rep(c("Massed", "Spaced"), each = 4), 3), levels = c("Massed", "Spaced")), score = c(4,5,7,8, 4,5,7,8, 6,7,9,10, 10,11,13,14, 8,9,11,12, 16,17,19,20)) massed <- subset(feedback_data, practice == "Massed") table(massed$feedback) #> #> Rereading Answer feedback Explanatory feedback #> 4 4 4 with(massed, tapply(score, feedback, mean)) #> Rereading Answer feedback Explanatory feedback #> 6 8 10 with(massed, tapply(score, feedback, sd)) #> Rereading Answer feedback Explanatory feedback #> 1.825741858 1.825741858 1.825741858 ``` ::: The Massed means are 6, 8 and 10 correct answers, with four pupils in each group and a sample SD of 1.8257 in every group. Their grand mean is 8. Before asking whether a difference is large relative to its uncertainty, we can see the difference on the outcome's own scale: Answer feedback exceeds Rereading by 2 points and Explanatory feedback exceeds it by 4 points. ### Extend a graph one useful component at a time Chapter 5 used base-R plotting functions. The package `ggplot2` provides another way to describe a graph: name a data frame, map its variables to visual properties, and add the kinds of marks that should be drawn. Its incremental advantage is that another layer or mapping can extend the same description without rebuilding the graph from separate drawing commands. Load this one package after its installation has been checked in the Computer Lab. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) p <- ggplot(massed, aes(feedback, score)) p + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](chapter_06_files/figure-html/ch06-first-ggplot-1.png){fig-alt='The first ggplot places the twelve Massed pupil scores in three vertical groups, labelled Rereading, Answer feedback and Explanatory feedback.' width=614.4} ::: ::: `ggplot(massed, ...)` supplies the records. Inside `aes()`, the feedback variable maps to horizontal position and score maps to vertical position. `geom_point()` adds one point for each record. The object `p` stores the data and mapping; the expression with `+` adds a plotting component. We can now add the three group means as larger diamonds. `aggregate()` uses the same twelve scores to make one mean per feedback group. The second point layer inherits the mapping from `p` but uses this three-row data frame. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} group_means <- aggregate(score ~ feedback, massed, mean) p + geom_point(size = 2) + geom_point(data = group_means, shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "black") + labs(x = "Feedback", y = "Number correct (out of 20)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Individual Massed scores and their three group means.](chapter_06_files/figure-html/fig-ch06-feedback-groups-1.png){#fig-ch06-feedback-groups fig-alt='Four scores in each of Rereading, Answer feedback and Explanatory feedback lie around means 6, 8 and 10. Larger diamonds mark the means; all groups have the same constructed spread.' width=614.4} ::: ::: The fixed colour is an argument outside `aes()`. Later, placing a variable inside `aes(colour = ...)` will give different colours to its levels and create a legend. `labs()` names the axes, and `theme_minimal()` changes their presentation. Neither changes the observations or the means. In @fig-ch06-feedback-groups the raw points keep the denominator and within-group variation visible beside the means. ### Fit the group model and read its decomposition For pupil $i$ in feedback group $j$, the one-way model is $$ Y_{ij}=\mu_j+\varepsilon_{ij}. $$ Here $\mu_j$ is the group's process mean and $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is its pupil's deviation from that mean. Fitting by least squares estimates each $\mu_j$ with the corresponding sample mean, so $\widehat Y_{ij}=\bar Y_j$. The residual is $e_{ij}=y_{ij}-\bar y_j$: an observed score minus its fitted group mean. For the first group the fitted values are all 6 and the residuals are $-2,-1,1,2$. The model lets us separate differences between groups from differences among pupils within a group. Chapter 4's decomposition becomes $$ \begin{aligned} SS_T&=\sum_{j}\sum_i(y_{ij}-\bar y)^2=SS_B+SS_W,\\ SS_B&=\sum_j n_j(\bar y_j-\bar y)^2,\\ SS_W&=\sum_j\sum_i(y_{ij}-\bar y_j)^2. \end{aligned} $$ The total measures deviation from the grand mean. The between-group term measures deviation of the three group means from that grand mean, weighted by their group counts. The within-group term measures deviation of pupils from their own fitted group means. In this example, $SS_B=4(6-8)^2+4(8-8)^2+4(10-8)^2=32$ and each group contributes $(-2)^2+(-1)^2+1^2+2^2=10$ to $SS_W$, giving $SS_W=30$. The formula `score ~ feedback` tells `aov()` to explain score using the feedback factor. `anova()` extracts the decomposition from the fitted object; `fitted()` and `resid()` expose its predicted values and residuals. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} one_fit <- aov(score ~ feedback, data = massed) anova(one_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

The within-group mean square $MS_W=30/9=3.3333$ estimates the common error variance. | Source | SS | df | MS | F | p | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Feedback | 32.0000 | 2 | 16.0000 | 4.8000 | .0381 | | Within groups | 30.0000 | 9 | 3.3333 | | | | Total | 62.0000 | 11 | | | | : One-way ANOVA on the twelve Massed pupils. {#tbl-ch06-oneway} The null hypothesis is $H_0:\mu_R=\mu_A=\mu_E$. Under independent Normal errors with a common variance, the ratio $$ F=\frac{MS_B}{MS_W}=\frac{16}{30/9}=4.8000 $$ has an $F_{2,9}$ reference distribution when that null holds. The p-value .0381 is the probability, under this null model, of an F statistic at least this large. At a .05 threshold it provides evidence against equal process means. It does not say that every pair differs, that all feedback improves performance, or that the invented result establishes a real intervention effect. The next section asks the individual comparison questions. The observed share of score variation associated with these group means is $$ \eta^2=\frac{SS_B}{SS_T}=\frac{32}{62}=.5161. $$ This is an in-sample variation summary, accompanying differences expressed in score points. It is neither the probability that feedback caused a result nor a replacement for a confidence interval. Appendix A gives the related bias-adjusted omega-squared calculation, with its denominator and interpretation. ### Express the same fit with indicators A factor with three levels can also enter a linear model as two indicator variables. Let $D_A=1$ for Answer feedback and 0 otherwise, and let $D_E=1$ for Explanatory feedback and 0 otherwise. Rereading has both indicators 0. The fitted equation is $$ \widehat y=6+2D_A+4D_E. $$ Substituting the indicators gives 6 for Rereading, $6+2=8$ for Answer feedback and $6+4=10$ for Explanatory feedback. The intercept is the reference mean; each other coefficient is a difference from that mean. The factor order in the original setup makes Rereading the reference level. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} indicator_fit <- lm(score ~ feedback, data = massed) coef(indicator_fit) #> (Intercept) feedbackAnswer feedback #> 6 2 #> feedbackExplanatory feedback #> 4 anova(indicator_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

::: ::: `lm()` and `aov()` describe the same set of fitted means and give the same residuals and ANOVA here. The formula names the outcome and explanatory variable; the study's design supplies the independence assumption. This indicator representation will make the adjusted group comparison easier to read. Chapter 7 develops a continuous predictor's slope, and Chapter 8 extends the conditional interpretation to several predictors. ## Ask comparisons within stated families {#ch06-contrast-families} ### Specify the comparison and its standard error Suppose the two questions concern Answer feedback versus Rereading and Explanatory feedback versus Rereading, among Massed pupils. In the order Rereading, Answer feedback, Explanatory feedback, their coefficient vectors are $(-1,1,0)$ and $(-1,0,1)$. Each vector sums to zero. A quantity $$ C=\sum_jc_j\mu_j,\qquad \sum_jc_j=0, $$ is a contrast of the process means. Its estimate replaces process means with the observed group means: $\widehat C=\sum_jc_j\bar y_j$. Thus our estimates are 2 and 4 points. Calling a comparison a contrast specifies this mathematical form; it does not say whether the comparison was planned before seeing the results or selected afterward. That is additional information about the analysis. For independent groups with a common error variance, Chapter 3's variance rule for a linear combination gives $$ SE(\widehat C)=\sqrt{MS_W\sum_j\frac{c_j^2}{n_j}}. $$ Each comparison uses two of the means, so both have estimated SE $\sqrt{(30/9)(1/4+1/4)}=1.2910$ points. The third group still contributes to the common error estimate and its 9 residual degrees of freedom. This matters when comparing these results with an analysis restricted to only two groups. ### Calibrate the two-comparison family An individual 95% interval uses a .05 error probability for that one comparison. To cover both declared comparisons with at least 95% familywise confidence, Bonferroni allocates .025 to each two-sided comparison. Each tail then receives $.05/(2\times2)=.0125$. The calibration uses the $t$ reference distribution with the model's 9 residual degrees of freedom [@student1908], giving the critical value $$ t_{1-.05/(2\times2),9}=2.6850. $$ The calculations retain the same estimates and SEs but multiply each SE by this larger critical value. The following code extracts the common variance estimate from the fitted object and calculates both results from unrounded inputs. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mse <- deviance(one_fit) / df.residual(one_fit) means <- with(massed, tapply(score, feedback, mean)) estimate <- c(Answer = unname(means[2] - means[1]), Explain = unname(means[3] - means[1])) se <- sqrt(mse * (1/4 + 1/4)) critical <- qt(1 - .05/(2*2), df.residual(one_fit)) raw_p <- 2 * pt(-abs(estimate/se), df.residual(one_fit)) cbind(estimate, SE = se, lower = estimate-critical*se, upper = estimate+critical*se, adjusted_p = p.adjust(raw_p, method = "bonferroni")) #> estimate SE lower upper #> Answer 2 1.290994449 -1.466334098 5.466334098 #> Explain 4 1.290994449 0.533665902 7.466334098 #> adjusted_p #> Answer 0.31148928496 #> Explain 0.02551124295 ``` ::: | Comparison | Estimate | SE | Simultaneous interval | Adjusted p | |:--|--:|--:|:--|--:| | Answer minus Rereading | 2.0000 | 1.2910 | [$-1.4663$, 5.4663] | .3115 | | Explanatory minus Rereading | 4.0000 | 1.2910 | [0.5337, 7.4663] | .0255 | : Bonferroni results for the declared family of two comparisons. {#tbl-ch06-bonferroni tbl-colwidths="[32,13,13,28,14]"} Multiplying each raw p-value by two and capping at one gives the corresponding Bonferroni-adjusted p-value. Explanatory minus Rereading is distinguishable from zero with this familywise calibration, whereas Answer minus Rereading is not. Its interval allows both a small negative difference and a positive difference of several points. This uncertainty is compatible with the earlier omnibus rejection: the omnibus test and each contrast address different statements. ### Compare with an all-pairs family If the question includes every pair, there are three comparisons. Tukey's procedure uses the joint distribution of pairwise mean differences under the common-variance Normal-error model. `TukeyHSD()` supplies those simultaneous intervals and their adjusted p-values [@tukey1953]. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} TukeyHSD(one_fit, "feedback", conf.level = .95) #> Tukey multiple comparisons of means #> 95% family-wise confidence level #> #> Fit: aov(formula = score ~ feedback, data = massed) #> #> $feedback #> diff lwr #> Answer feedback-Rereading 2 -1.6044637455 #> Explanatory feedback-Rereading 4 0.3955362545 #> Explanatory feedback-Answer feedback 2 -1.6044637455 #> upr p adj #> Answer feedback-Rereading 5.604463746 0.3149864972 #> Explanatory feedback-Rereading 7.604463746 0.0310140456 #> Explanatory feedback-Answer feedback 5.604463746 0.3149864972 ``` ::: The output labels each subtraction direction. Explanatory minus Rereading is 4, with interval [0.3955, 7.6045] and adjusted p .0310. Answer minus Rereading and Explanatory minus Answer both equal 2, with intervals [$-1.6045$, 5.6045] and adjusted p .3150. These limits differ from the preceding intervals because the declared family and its calibration differ. An interval should therefore be read together with the comparison and family it represents. An omnibus rejection does not by itself protect any comparison selected after examining the means. Conversely, a separately specified contrast can have its own valid uncertainty procedure without requiring omnibus rejection as an automatic preliminary gate. The relevant information is the question, selection process and calibration, rather than a universal sequence of significance decisions. ### Check what changes when the variance model changes The common-variance model assumes that within-group variability estimates one shared error variance. In a real study, design information and observed patterns help assess that working model. A small normality or variance test cannot certify it, especially with four pupils per group. Here the identical SDs were deliberately constructed. For independent groups whose error variances may differ, Welch's one-way procedure provides an alternative [@welch1947]. R selects it by default in `oneway.test()` [@rcore2025]: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} oneway.test(score ~ feedback, data = massed) #> #> One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances) #> #> data: score and feedback #> F = 4.32, num df = 2, denom df = 6, p-value = 0.06883836 ``` ::: It gives $F(2,6)=4.3200$, p .0688. Although the observed group SDs happen to be equal, Welch's small-sample correction and reference degrees of freedom differ from the pooled-variance ANOVA. Its uncertainty calculation is built for a different variance model. The two p-values are therefore results to explain through their assumptions and calibration, rather than votes on which numerical conclusion to prefer. With small groups, the model choice can matter appreciably. A useful exact identity connects a two-group pooled t test with a two-group ANOVA: $F=t^2$, with the same two-sided p-value. It requires the same records, equal-variance denominator and group comparison. R's default Welch t test does not meet that specification. Nor is our three-group contrast the same calculation, because it uses residual information from the third group. Appendix A reproduces the matched identity explicitly. ## Compare a two-way pattern {#ch06-factorial-comparisons} ### Read cells and margins before fitting We now return to all 24 pupils and ask how the Spaced-minus-Massed comparison changes across feedback conditions. A cell is one combination of feedback and practice. Computing cell counts and means first makes the six cells and their denominators visible. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} with(feedback_data, table(feedback, practice)) #> practice #> feedback Massed Spaced #> Rereading 4 4 #> Answer feedback 4 4 #> Explanatory feedback 4 4 cell_mean <- with(feedback_data, tapply(score, list(feedback, practice), mean)) cell_mean #> Massed Spaced #> Rereading 6 6 #> Answer feedback 8 12 #> Explanatory feedback 10 18 rowMeans(cell_mean) #> Rereading Answer feedback Explanatory feedback #> 6 10 14 colMeans(cell_mean) #> Massed Spaced #> 8 12 mean(feedback_data$score) #> [1] 10 ``` ::: | Feedback | Massed | Spaced | Equally weighted margin | Spaced minus Massed | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Rereading | 6 | 6 | 6 | 0 | | Answer feedback | 8 | 12 | 10 | 4 | | Explanatory feedback | 10 | 18 | 14 | 8 | | Practice margin | 8 | 12 | 10 | 4 | : Cell means and equally weighted margins of the balanced design. {#tbl-ch06-cell-means tbl-colwidths="[31,12,12,23,22]"} Each cell has four pupils, so averaging the two practice cells equally gives the feedback group's overall mean. Similarly, each practice margin averages equally across the three feedback conditions. In an unbalanced design, a margin must specify its weights: the observed mix of pupils and an equally weighted target can answer different questions. The new graph uses the same data/mapping/layer idea as the earlier group plot. Here a colour identifies each feedback condition and `group` identifies the means to connect. The line joins separate cell means; it does not trace individual pupils across repeated measurements. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cell_plot <- aggregate(score ~ feedback + practice, feedback_data, mean) ggplot(cell_plot, aes(practice, score, colour = feedback, group = feedback)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) + labs(x = "Practice", y = "Mean number correct", colour = "Feedback") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The practice difference depends on feedback.](chapter_06_files/figure-html/fig-ch06-feedback-interaction-1.png){#fig-ch06-feedback-interaction fig-alt='Rereading joins 6 to 6, Answer feedback joins 8 to 12, and Explanatory feedback joins 10 to 18 from Massed to Spaced. The lines have different slopes.' width=614.4} ::: ::: `colour = feedback` is inside `aes()` because a variable now determines colour. The mapping also creates the legend. The observed changes are 0, 4 and 8 points, producing nonparallel lines in @fig-ch06-feedback-interaction. This describes interaction in the observed means. Inference about a process interaction additionally requires a model and a measure of residual variation. ### Fit the full model and identify its tests Chapter 4 wrote the two-way model as $$ Y_{ijk}=\mu+\alpha_j+\beta_k+(\alpha\beta)_{jk} +\varepsilon_{ijk}, $$ where $j$ indexes feedback, $k$ indexes practice and $i$ indexes pupils within a cell. With the usual sum-to-zero constraints, $\mu$ is the grand mean, $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_k$ describe departures of the margins from it, and $(\alpha\beta)_{jk}$ describes the remaining cell departure. The constraints make this representation identifiable: the effects cannot all shift freely while leaving the same fitted means. There is one grand-mean parameter, $3-1=2$ feedback degrees of freedom, $2-1=1$ practice degree of freedom, and $(3-1)(2-1)=2$ interaction degrees of freedom. Together these describe six fitted cell means. The model therefore has $24-6=18$ residual degrees of freedom. In an R formula, `feedback * practice` includes both main effects and their interaction. It expands to `feedback + practice + feedback:practice`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} two_fit <- aov(score ~ feedback * practice, data = feedback_data) anova(two_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

The practice test concerns equality of practice margins averaged equally over feedback. The interaction test asks whether the practice difference is the same across all feedback conditions. With independent Normal errors of common variance, its null reference is $F_{2,18}$; the observed value 9.6000 and p .0015 provide evidence against that common-difference null. The balanced layout makes the source components orthogonal: the variation attributed to one component does not compete with another component for the same fitted direction. A single-model `anova()` table ordinarily uses sequential sums of squares, entering terms in formula order. This convenient balanced decomposition should not be extended automatically to unbalanced or adjusted data. Later in this chapter, we compare explicitly named nested models on identical rows to specify adjusted questions. The feedback and practice margins remain meaningful descriptions, but the interaction clarifies their limits. For example, the 4-point overall practice difference averages a 0-point, a 4-point and an 8-point difference. A result paragraph should convey this varying pattern when the scientific question concerns how practice works across feedback conditions. ### Work the selected difference of differences completely Consider Answer feedback's practice change minus Rereading's practice change: $$ \widehat{DD}=(12-8)-(6-6)=4. $$ The contrast has coefficients $(1,-1,-1,1)$ in the cell order Rereading–Massed, Rereading–Spaced, Answer–Massed, Answer–Spaced. Its four cell means come from different pupils. Under the common-variance model, their variances therefore add after multiplying by the squared coefficients: $$ SE(\widehat{DD})= \sqrt{MS_E\left(\frac14+\frac14+\frac14+\frac14\right)} =1.8257. $$ The omnibus interaction spans two independent directions. For simultaneous confidence over all contrasts in that two-dimensional interaction space, Scheffe's method uses the multiplier $$ \sqrt{2F_{.95;2,18}}=2.6663. $$ The complete calculation keeps the cell subtraction, residual variance and family calibration visible: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dd <- (cell_mean["Answer feedback", "Spaced"] - cell_mean["Answer feedback", "Massed"]) - (cell_mean["Rereading", "Spaced"] - cell_mean["Rereading", "Massed"]) mse_two <- deviance(two_fit) / df.residual(two_fit) se_dd <- sqrt(mse_two * 4/4) scheffe <- sqrt(2 * qf(.95, 2, 18)) c(estimate = dd, SE = se_dd, multiplier = scheffe) #> estimate SE multiplier #> 4.000000000 1.825741858 2.666292237 dd + c(-1, 1) * scheffe * se_dd #> [1] -0.8679613431 8.8679613431 ``` ::: The resulting interval is $4\pm2.6663(1.8257)=[-0.8680,8.8680]$. It includes zero even though the interaction F test rejects its null. The F test asks whether both interaction directions are zero jointly; this interval addresses one selected direction while allowing for the entire family. Other directions can carry substantial evidence, and a simultaneous interval for this direction can remain broad. Neither result cancels the other. Three related quantities help distinguish the questions. Answer feedback's simple practice effect is 4, with SE 1.2910 and pointwise t interval [1.2877, 6.7123]. The selected DD also happens to equal 4, but its SE is 1.8257 because it compares two practice effects. Its pointwise interval is [0.1643, 7.8357], whereas its simultaneous interval is [$-0.8680$, 8.8680]. Appendix A shows both DD calculations using the same estimate and SE. A simple effect includes the overall practice component as well as an interaction component. It is therefore outside the interaction-only family used above. The shared numerical estimate does not give it the DD's meaning, SE or familywise guarantee. Chapter 3 introduced the invented completion table in @tbl-ch06-completion-counts. It contains aggregate counts for 100 records, classified by learning format and completion. These records have no pupil-level linkage to either feedback dataset above. The counts themselves establish neither random allocation nor representative sampling. | Format | Completed | Not completed | Total | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | Online | 32 | 18 | 50 | | In person | 18 | 32 | 50 | | Total | 50 | 50 | 100 | : The same authored completion counts as Chapter 3. {#tbl-ch06-completion-counts} For the Online group, the event is completion and the denominator is its 50 records. Under an independent Bernoulli model with a common completion probability $p$, the count of completions has a binomial distribution. The estimated probability is $\widehat p=32/50=.6400$. If records were clustered within dependent classes or came from repeated observations of the same people, this ordinary independent-unit uncertainty model would require modification. Suppose the benchmark is $p_0=.5$. The score test standardizes the difference using the variance under that null: $$ z=\frac{\widehat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/50}} =\frac{.64-.5}{\sqrt{.5(.5)/50}}=1.9799. $$ Squaring gives $X^2=z^2=3.9200$, compared with a chi-squared distribution on one degree of freedom. The procedure uses a large-sample reference; the expected numbers of successes and failures under this null are both 25. \Needspace{17\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} one_prop <- prop.test(32, 50, p = .5, correct = FALSE) one_prop$estimate #> p #> 0.64 one_prop$statistic #> X-squared #> 3.92 one_prop$p.value #> [1] 0.04771488024 one_prop$conf.int #> [1] 0.5014101688 0.7586125035 #> attr(,"conf.level") #> [1] 0.95 ``` ::: The two-sided p-value is .0477. The estimated completion probability is .6400, with 95% Wilson score interval [.5014, .7586]. `correct = FALSE` explicitly selects the uncorrected score procedure; accepting R's default continuity correction would specify a different calculation. The call and the reported result should identify which procedure was used. The score interval contains the candidate probabilities that their own two-sided score tests would retain [@wilson1927]. Each candidate supplies the variance for its null calculation. This inversion explains why the interval is linked to the score test and is not simply $\widehat p\pm1.96\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/n}$, the Wald interval. Appendix A gives the Wilson endpoints directly. The p-value assesses the stipulated benchmark; it is not the probability that $p=.5$ is true or a measure of the completion rate's practical importance. ### Compare the two groups through their full table Now ask whether completion probability differs by format. This uses both rows and a different null: format and completion are independent in the working population model, equivalently equal completion probabilities in this two-group setting. Constructing labelled counts prevents an accidental change in the event or group direction. \Needspace{28\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts <- matrix(c(32, 18, 18, 32), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(Format = c("Online", "In person"), Result = c("Completed", "Not completed"))) counts #> Result #> Format Completed Not completed #> Online 32 18 #> In person 18 32 prop.table(counts, margin = 1) #> Result #> Format Completed Not completed #> Online 0.64 0.36 #> In person 0.36 0.64 count_test <- chisq.test(counts, correct = FALSE) count_test$expected #> Result #> Format Completed Not completed #> Online 25 25 #> In person 25 25 count_test$statistic #> X-squared #> 7.84 count_test$p.value #> [1] 0.005110260661 count_test$residuals #> Result #> Format Completed Not completed #> Online 1.4 -1.4 #> In person -1.4 1.4 ``` ::: `margin = 1` divides each row by its own total. Completion rates are .6400 for Online and .3600 for In person, a difference of .2800, or 28.0000 percentage points, in the Online-minus-In-person direction. Under independence the fitted expected count in row $j$, column $k$ is $$ E_{jk}=\frac{(\text{row }j\text{ total}) (\text{column }k\text{ total})}{N}. $$ All four expected counts here equal $50\times50/100=25$. Pearson's statistic accumulates the squared discrepancies relative to those expected counts: $$ X^2=\sum_{j,k}\frac{(O_{jk}-E_{jk})^2}{E_{jk}} =4\left(\frac{7^2}{25}\right)=7.8400. $$ For a $J$-by-$K$ table the usual independence reference has $(J-1)(K-1)$ degrees of freedom. Here $df=1$ and p .0051. The observed Pearson statistic $X^2$ is a number calculated from the table; $\chi^2_1$ names its approximate reference distribution under the null model. The Pearson residuals are $(O-E)/\sqrt E$: 1.4, $-1.4$, $-1.4$, 1.4 in row order. Their signs locate the pattern: more Online completions and fewer Online non-completions than the independence fit predicts, with the opposite departures for In person. Squaring and adding these residuals recovers $X^2$. They are related through the table margins, so their signs do not constitute four independent cell tests. The approximation concerns expected counts under the fitted null model, along with independent observational units and a sampling model appropriate to the table. Looking only at observed cell counts misses part of this check. Sparse expected cells may require an alternative reference or a more careful model. In the present example all expected counts are 25, supporting the ordinary chi-squared approximation under the stated unit model. The one-proportion test asked whether Online completion probability equals a fixed .5 benchmark. The complete-table test asks whether the two format probabilities are equal; it estimates their common probability under the null from the full table. Their different p-values answer different questions. Neither test establishes that changing format would cause completion to change without relevant design information. ### Use alternatives as changes to a stated analysis {#ch06-categorical-reference} The Computer Lab's categorical reference compares the two-proportion interface, a continuity-corrected calculation, Fisher's conditional test [@fisher1935] and a standardized association summary, Cramer's V [@cramer1946], using the same table. The small invented completion table above supplies the first complete procedure; the reference shows how method choice and unresolved source information matter in an existing dataset. ## Fit by an objective function and likelihood {#ch06-likelihood} ### Fix the data and vary a candidate parameter The fitted means in Section 1 were chosen by a rule: minimize the sum of squared deviations from the observations. We can inspect this rule with the four Massed Rereading scores, 4, 5, 7 and 8. These observations stay fixed. What changes is the proposed center, denoted by $c$. An **objective function** assigns a numerical criterion to each candidate parameter value for fixed data. For a center fitted by least squares, the objective is $$ Q(c)=\sum_{i=1}^{4}(y_i-c)^2 =(4-c)^2+(5-c)^2+(7-c)^2+(8-c)^2. $$ At $c=6$, the squared deviations sum to $4+1+1+4=10.0000$ squared score points. At either 5 or 7, they sum to 14.0000. Chapter 2 showed why the sample mean minimizes this criterion. Here the mean is 6.0000 points. A numerical search lets us reproduce the minimizing value without writing it into the fitting instruction. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rereading <- subset(massed, feedback == "Rereading")$score loss <- function(center) sum((rereading - center)^2) mean_fit <- optimize(loss, interval = range(rereading)) c(center = mean_fit$minimum, squared_loss = mean_fit$objective) #> center squared_loss #> 6 10 c(loss_at_5 = loss(5), loss_at_6 = loss(6), loss_at_7 = loss(7)) #> loss_at_5 loss_at_6 loss_at_7 #> 14 10 14 ``` ::: `function(center)` makes an R function whose input is a candidate center. Subtracting it from the vector forms four deviations; squaring and summing returns one number. `optimize()` searches for a minimum of that function over the interval supplied. Here `range(rereading)` gives $[4,8]$, which contains the sample mean. The objective is a single smooth bowl over this interval, so the scalar search has one minimum to locate. The two returned quantities have different meanings. `minimum` is the **parameter location**, 6.0000 points; `objective` is the function value there, 10.0000 squared points. The latter is a sum of squared deviations, not an SE or an estimate of the mean. The search interval also belongs to the fitting instruction: excluding the best center would restrict which answer the search could return. Numerical stopping tolerance concerns the accuracy of that search; statistical uncertainty concerns what an estimate would do across the repetitions justified by the study. These least-squares identities are arithmetic. An uncertainty statement for the fitted mean adds a model or design and its conditions. Chapter 7 extends this criterion from one center to a line with an intercept and slope. The Computer Lab reference varies the search interval while keeping the observations fixed. ### Change the fitting criterion for a binomial outcome For the completion example, the observations are 32 completions in 50 Online trials. Let $p$ denote a candidate probability of completion. Under the stipulated model of independent trials with a common probability, the number completed follows a binomial distribution. The model assigns probability $$ P_p(X=32)={50\choose32}p^{32}(1-p)^{18}. $$ In a probability calculation, we choose a value of $p$ and consider which counts might occur. For fitting, we have already observed the count: 32 stays fixed, as does the total of 50. We now evaluate the same expression at different candidate values of $p$. Viewed in this direction, it is the **likelihood function**, $$ L(p)={50\choose32}p^{32}(1-p)^{18},\qquad 0\le p\le1. $$ The binomial coefficient counts the ways 32 completions can occur among 50 trials. It is constant as $p$ varies. In this binomial model, likelihood is the probability of the observed data under each candidate model parameter; it is not a probability distribution over that parameter. In particular, a high likelihood at a candidate $p$ does not give the probability that $p$ is true. **Maximum likelihood estimation** chooses the parameter value that makes the observed data most likely under the declared model. The logarithm is increasing, so maximizing the log-likelihood gives the same parameter value. For $0 numerical analytic negative_loglik #> 0.6400059479 0.6400000000 2.1465474559 negative_loglik(.5) #> [1] 4.13299674 ``` ::: `dbinom()` evaluates the binomial probability for the fixed count 32. With `log = TRUE`, it computes the log probability directly. The numerical and analytic estimates both round to .6400. The small numerical difference from exactly .64 reflects the search tolerance. At the fitted probability the negative log-likelihood is 2.1465, compared with 4.1330 at $p=.5$. The smaller value is the better fit according to this criterion. The parameter estimate .6400 is a completion probability; the criterion value 2.1465 is not. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The binomial log-likelihood is largest at the observed proportion.](chapter_06_files/figure-html/fig-ch06-likelihood-1.png){#fig-ch06-likelihood fig-pos='H' fig-alt='For 32 successes in 50 fixed trials, the log-likelihood curve peaks at candidate probability .64. A dashed line at .5 intersects the curve at a lower value.' width=585.6} ::: ::: The horizontal axis contains candidate parameter values, and the vertical axis gives the log-likelihood of the same observed count at each candidate. Thus the curve displays a fitting criterion, not a sampling distribution or a distribution of probabilities over $p$. The peak identifies the fitted value. The score test and interval in Section 5 answer additional questions about a proposed null and the uncertainty of estimation under their stated calibration. Finally, check the boundaries of the parameter space. With both completions and non-completions observed, $p=0$ and $p=1$ each give likelihood zero, so the maximum is interior. If all 50 trials instead had zero completions, the maximum would be at $p=0$; if all completed, it would be at $p=1$. An interior numerical search can approach such an endpoint without returning it exactly. The endpoint values must therefore be examined explicitly in those cases. Both estimated rates are close to .05. The **power** column estimates the probability of rejecting that same null under the specified unequal means. It rises from .6545 with four pupils per group to .9990 with 12. This is power against the particular means 6, 8 and 10, with the stated spread and independence; a smaller separation would give different power. Each rate is itself an estimate based on finitely many repetitions. If $\hat q$ is a simulated rejection proportion from $B$ independent studies, its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is $$ MCSE(\hat q)=\sqrt{\frac{\hat q(1-\hat q)}{B}}. $$ For the estimated power .6545, the calculation is: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sqrt(.6545 * (1 - .6545) / 2000) #> [1] 0.01063319684 ``` ::: The result, 0.0106, describes the numerical uncertainty from using 2,000 simulations. A fresh set of 2,000 simulated studies can give a somewhat different power estimate. This MCSE is distinct from a pupil outcome's SD or the SE of a group mean or contrast within one study. A rate very close to one, such as .9990, also deserves care: only two of the 2,000 studies failed to reject, so its tiny plug-in MCSE rests on very few non-rejections. Increasing the number of pupils $n$ changes the information within a study, its error degrees of freedom and its ability to detect the specified difference. Increasing the number of repetitions $B$ makes the simulated rate more precise; it leaves the study being simulated unchanged. The Computer Lab develops these changes in the repetition task and its reference extension. Simulation describes a procedure under the declared model; agreement with its expected behaviour does not establish that the model fits a particular real study. ### Plan for a specified comparison and precision target The omnibus simulation asks whether some population group means differ. A future study may instead be planned to estimate or detect one particular difference. Return to the two comparisons with Rereading from the one-way example: Answer feedback versus Rereading, and Explanatory feedback versus Rereading. Keep this declared **two-comparison Bonferroni family**, with family significance level .05, even when calculating power for just one of its comparisons. Suppose the comparison of interest has a population difference of $\delta=2$ points. Plan equal group sizes $n$, independent Normal outcomes and common SD $\sigma=\sqrt{10/3}$. The planning SE for a difference of two group means is $\sigma\sqrt{2/n}$. All three groups contribute to the pooled error variance, so its degrees of freedom are $3(n-1)$, even though the contrast compares only two of the means. Bonferroni assigns two-sided significance level $.05/2=.025$ to each comparison. Dividing that amount between its two tails puts .0125 in each tail. The rejection cutoffs are therefore $-c$ and $c$, where $$ c=t_{1-.05/(2\times2),\,3(n-1)}=t_{.9875,\,3(n-1)}. $$ Under the zero-difference null, the test statistic has the central $t$ distribution already used for the comparison. Under a specified nonzero difference, its distribution moves towards that difference. The **noncentral $t$ distribution** describes this statistic when its numerator has a nonzero mean and its denominator still estimates the common spread. Its noncentrality parameter expresses the population difference in planning SE units: $$ \lambda=\frac{\delta}{\sigma\sqrt{2/n}}. $$ For this alternative, power is the area beyond the same two rejection cutoffs: $P(T<-c)+P(T>c)$ for a noncentral $t$ variable with $3(n-1)$ degrees of freedom and noncentrality $\lambda$. These are probabilities over future studies, rather than a p-value from observed data. Both tails belong to the two-sided procedure, even when the planning difference is positive. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} contrast_power <- function(n, delta = 2, sigma = sqrt(10/3)) { df <- 3*(n-1) critical <- qt(1 - .05/(2*2), df) ncp <- delta / (sigma * sqrt(2/n)) pt(-critical, df, ncp = ncp) + pt(critical, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE) } round(c(n16 = contrast_power(16), n17 = contrast_power(17)), 4) #> n16 n17 #> 0.7793 0.8073 ``` ::: The function accepts a proposed group size and returns power. Its first `pt()` call obtains the lower-tail probability; the second obtains the upper-tail probability. At $n=17$, the planning SE is 0.6262, the error degrees of freedom are 48, the critical value is 2.3139, and $\lambda=2/0.6262\approx3.1937$. Summing the two tail areas gives power .8073. Checking successive integer sizes gives 17 pupils per group, 51 in total, as the first size reaching .80 power; 16 gives .7793. This is the power of **one specified comparison within the declared family**. It is neither the probability that both comparisons reject nor the power of the omnibus F test. For example, with 12 pupils per group the specified two-point comparison has power .6328, whereas the omnibus simulation in @tbl-ch06-simulation gives estimated power .9990 against the complete pattern $(6,8,10)$. The hypotheses and rejection rules differ, so these numbers answer different questions. A precision target concerns the interval's width rather than its probability of excluding zero. Suppose the aim is a simultaneous interval whose planned half-width is no more than one point. The family and degrees of freedom stay the same, giving $$ \text{planned half-width} =t_{.9875,\,3(n-1)}\,\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}. $$ This calculation substitutes the planning SD $\sigma$ for the error SD that the future study will estimate. Evaluating the two sizes either side of the threshold gives: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_width <- c(34, 35) round(data.frame( n = n_width, planned_half_width = qt(1 - .05/(2*2), 3*(n_width-1)) * sqrt(2*(10/3)/n_width) ), 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| n| planned_half_width| |--:|------------------:| | 34| 1.0078| | 35| 0.9929|
::: ::: The first group size meeting this planning target is 35, or 105 pupils in total: the planned half-width is 0.9929 points, compared with 1.0078 at 34. The realised interval uses the observed $\sqrt{MS_E}$ and therefore has a random width. Choosing 35 does not guarantee that its half-width will be at most one in every study. @fig-ch06-planning shows why a power target and an interval-width target can select quite different sample sizes. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Power and planned interval width impose different sample-size targets.](chapter_06_files/figure-html/fig-ch06-planning-1.png){#fig-ch06-planning fig-alt='For the same two-comparison three-group procedure, power rises above .8 at 17 pupils per group. Planned simultaneous interval half-width falls below one point at 35 pupils per group.' width=614.4} ::: ::: Finally, distinguish the desired number of available outcomes from the number recruited. If outcomes are expected to be available for 90% of recruits, the 17-per-group power target gives: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ceiling(17 / .9) #> [1] 19 ``` ::: Recruiting 19 per group gives 57 recruits and an expected 17.1 available outcomes per group under that retention assumption. It is an average allowance, not a guarantee of 17 outcomes in every group or a correction for bias from systematically missing outcomes. The following concepts were introduced or developed through their R applications here. | Term | Definition | |:--|:--| | ANCOVA (analysis of covariance) | A linear model comparing groups while including quantitative covariates; its adjusted comparison is defined at stated covariate values or over a stated covariate distribution. | | Model formula (R formula) | Notation such as `score ~ group` naming an outcome and the variables that explain it for a fitting function. It does not state whether observations are independent or paired; that comes from the design. | | Objective function | A numerical criterion evaluated at candidate parameter values for fixed data; fitting seeks a stated minimum or maximum. | | Likelihood and log-likelihood | The probability or density of the observed data under a declared model, viewed as a function of its parameters; the log-likelihood is its logarithm. | | Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) | Choosing parameter values that maximize the likelihood, equivalently the log-likelihood, over the stated parameter space. | : Selected concepts introduced or developed here. {#tbl-ch06-terms tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"} The notation follows the local question. $C=\sum_jc_j\mu_j$ is a contrast, whereas $L(\theta)$ is a likelihood function of a parameter. Similarly, Type II error probability $\beta$ differs from a model coefficient such as $\beta_x$. Observed Pearson $X^2$ differs from the reference distribution $\chi^2$. In simulations, $n$ counts observations per stated study or group and $B$ counts repeated studies. An SE describes an estimator's sampling variation; an MCSE describes finite-simulation uncertainty in a computed summary. ### Further reading {.unnumbered} For the linear-model basis of ANOVA, contrasts and covariance adjustment, see @kutner2005. @tukey1953 develops simultaneous comparison ideas, and @wilson1927 provides the score-interval construction for a proportion. @cohen1988 discusses power and the dependence of a planning result on its chosen effect and procedure, and @cetinkaya2024 develops the simulation-based treatment of operating characteristics used in Section 7. The following calculation reconstructs all three sums of squares and the observed eta-squared summary. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grand <- mean(massed$score) ss_between <- sum(4 * (means-grand)^2) ss_within <- sum(resid(one_fit)^2) ss_total <- sum((massed$score-grand)^2) c(SS_B = ss_between, SS_W = ss_within, SS_T = ss_total, eta2 = ss_between/ss_total) #> SS_B SS_W SS_T eta2 #> 32.0000000000 30.0000000000 62.0000000000 0.5161290323 ``` ::: The values 32, 30 and 62 reproduce the main table, with $32+30=62$ and $\eta^2=.5161$. For this one-way model, a conventional bias-adjusted variance-share estimator is $$ \widehat\omega^2= \frac{SS_B-(J-1)MS_W}{SS_T+MS_W} =\frac{32-2(30/9)}{62+30/9}=.3878. $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (ss_between - 2*mse) / (ss_total + mse) #> [1] 0.387755102 ``` ::: Subtracting the error contribution from the numerator makes the estimate smaller here. In a sample with little between-group variation, that numerator can be negative. A negative estimate is a consequence of the bias adjustment, not a negative population variance share. Report the convention used if a display truncates it to zero. As with eta-squared, omega-squared does not replace the outcome-scale differences, their intervals or the design conditions for interpreting them. ### Match the two-group t and F calculations {.unnumbered} Restrict the Massed records to Rereading and Answer feedback. A pooled equal-variance t test and a two-group ANOVA then use the same eight pupils, two fitted means and six residual degrees of freedom. \Needspace{20\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} two_groups <- droplevels(subset(massed, feedback %in% c("Rereading", "Answer feedback"))) pooled <- t.test(score ~ feedback, data = two_groups, var.equal = TRUE) two_group_fit <- aov(score ~ feedback, data = two_groups) c(t = unname(pooled$statistic), t_squared = unname(pooled$statistic)^2, p = pooled$p.value) #> t t_squared p #> -1.5491933385 2.4000000000 0.1723082967 anova(two_group_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | Df| Sum Sq| Mean Sq| F value| Pr(>F)| |:---------|--:|------:|-----------:|-------:|------------:| |feedback | 1| 8| 8.000000000| 2.4| 0.1723082967| |Residuals | 6| 20| 3.333333333| NA| NA|

Inverting the score inequality gives a center and half-width $$ \begin{aligned} \text{center}&=\frac{\widehat p+z^2/(2n)}{1+z^2/n},\\ \text{half-width}&= \frac{z\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/n+z^2/(4n^2)}}{1+z^2/n}. \end{aligned} $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} phat <- 32/50 z <- qnorm(.975) center <- (phat + z^2/(2*50)) / (1 + z^2/50) half <- z * sqrt(phat*(1-phat)/50 + z^2/(4*50^2)) / (1 + z^2/50) center + c(-1, 1)*half #> [1] 0.5014101688 0.7586125035 ``` ::: The endpoints [.5014, .7586] reproduce the uncorrected one-proportion `prop.test()` interval.
